:knowledge-point/_canonical-example.:knowledge-point/title: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem in Flux Form

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0), (-1,-3), (1,-3),$ and $(1,0),$  traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (7x^2y^6 +x^3)\, \mathbf{i} + (- 2xy^7+4x^2y) \, \mathbf{j}$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/02/02964b07e45daba2d560fa16d34bcc92ddb8d0e0e83f644f8284dbe9d4b4557b.png)

We have that $P(x,y) =  7x^2y^6 +x^3$ and $Q(x,y) =- 2xy^7+4x^2y.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=14x{y}^{6}+3{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-14x{y}^{6}+4{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D = \{(x,y) :  -1\leq x\leq 1, \, -3\leq y \leq 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(14x{y}^{6}+3{x}^{2})+(-14x{y}^{6}+4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-3}^{0}7{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field 
$F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}+1,\,{y}^{2}⟩$
across the triangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),$ and $(0,2)$ can be represented as

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/c3/c3c617522488e6ebf47dd2b2a52c43a1fe06ccaef8cd1e8752ab4df5e2d4bd64.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+1$ and $Q(x,y)={y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2(x+y).$
